To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the eye is specified in the second larva and not in the embryo; that the eyeless gene is required to specify eye identity in response to EGF receptor signaling and Notch signaling; that EGF receptor and Notch signaling act upstream of the eyeless gene; and that the expression of the eyeless and pax6 genes in the second larvalsegment is not sufficient to specify eye identity.

1) the EGF Reaction and Notch signaling are required for eye development; 2) the EGF reaction and Notch signaling act upstream of the Eyeless/Pax 6 and Sine oculis/Otx genes; and 3) the eye is specified in the second larva stage.
EGF Receptor signaling and the Notch pathway control the expression of Eyeless/PAX6, which in turn controls the development of the Drosophila eye.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms that specify cell fates in Drosophila.
the genetic control of development in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, and specifically the development of the compound eye.
the genetic mechanisms of pattern formation in the eye and brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the eye specification genes are necessary, but not sufficient for eye development, and that the EGF receptor and Notch signaling act upstream of the eye genes.
the EGF receptor and Notch signaling act upstream of Eyeless/PAX6 to control eye specification.
the EGF receptor and Notch signaling pathway act upstream of eyeless/Pax6 and that eye specification occurs much later in development.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the EGF and Notch signaling cascades are required to establish the identity of the presumptive eye, and that the eye specification genes act in a combinatorial manner to specify the eye.
the eye specification genes act in a cascade that is activated by the EGF Receptors and Notch signaling pathway.
EGF Receptor/Notch signaling acts upstream of the Eyeless/Pax-6 pathway to specify eye identity in the second larva.
The main takeaway from our work is that
eye development is not controlled by a single master control protein but by a network of interacting signaling pathways.
the eye specification genes are neither necessary nor sufficient to specify the eye in all cases.
the eye specification genes do not act in concert to control eye development.
